sb_prompt: FIND OUT WHAT EVERYDAY OCCURRENCES THE OTHER CALLER CONSIDERS TO BE AN INTRUSION OF PRIVACY.  WHAT CAN BE DONE TO PREVENT THEM?  DO YOU AGREE OR DISAGREE?
turns: Yeah, so like, do you think tracking where you go in your own car is a big deal?

I mean, honestly? Yeah, it feels like an invasion. My mom told me once her car was being tracked after she got into a minor fender bender with a junkie, and suddenly she was getting calls from police she never asked for.
That's really messed up, I totally get why you'd feel violated, especially since I've had a friend who was in that exact situation and she still gets shivers thinking about it.

Yeah, it's just the whole idea that you don't even know who's looking... like, if your kid texts "I'm late" and your GPS pops up on your wife's phone, is that creepy or helpful? I feel like it depends on who's driving the car.
It's creepy if your spouse is spying without asking, but if it's a kid in an emergency, I say it's necessary to know they're safe.
It is, right? Just having the knowledge that every trip you make is being logged feels like someone is watching you all the time.

Right, but do you think people should even have that option if they don't want it? My friend just begged me to turn it off for her shift because she hates knowing where the company is watching her, but I'm not sure my boss would let her.

Yeah, I guess it's a tough spot. If you're working in a car for your job, like driving a route or making deliveries, I think the company needs to know where you are for your own safety, but maybe they should stop logging every single second if you're just parked for coffee. You know, like, "You've been there for twenty minutes, yeah, you're probably taking a break, let's stop tracking." But if you're actively driving a patient or a client, that feels totally different and necessary.
That actually makes sense, because my friend is a nurse too, and she's always terrified of someone just following her shifts to find out where she lives or what she's doing on her days off.

Yeah, that scares me too, because I have a friend who's a teacher and she said her GPS was on and some random guy was tailing her while she drove her students around to the field trip. She never knew where we were going until she checked the map on her phone.

Right, but wait—if a teacher is driving on a field trip, isn't that technically company time? Or do they own the bus? My friend said the GPS was on her personal phone though, which is where it gets weird.

Yeah, but it's not even the school bus that's the issue, it was her own personal phone. She didn't have a GPS for the school, she just had her kid's app on her own phone and somehow it started broadcasting her location to her principal's email address every ten minutes.
That sounds insane, like a creepy stalker move if you ask me.
That is wild, and honestly it sounds like your friend should have just turned off the app if it was sending data to a principal anyway.

Yeah, that's actually the worst part—I mean, if the kid set it up, maybe it's fine, but if it's a random app that just leaks it to *anyone* who finds the code, that's insane. Did she try to shut it down yet?

Yeah, she tried to wipe her location history but apparently the school had a backup somewhere, so now she just keeps her phone on airplane mode when she's not actively with the kids, which is kind of annoying since she's a librarian and people ask where I am all the time anyway.
Yeah, that's just why I'm paranoid about my own car; I swear I have to turn it off before I leave the parking lot or someone will know exactly where I'm sleeping.
Yeah, airplane mode is a pain though, because if my kid actually texts me from somewhere weird, I can't even see it until I land back home.
Yeah, I guess that's why I keep my phone on airplane whenever I'm clocking out at the hospital, even if it means I miss a text from my daughter for a few hours.
That's just it, isn't? I mean, if I can't see where my kid is until it's too late, am I actually protecting them or just ignoring the warning signs?

Yeah, but then my daughter called me yesterday saying she was lost and I didn't get the alert until ten minutes later because the battery died while it was in airplane mode... and honestly, now I don't know if I'm keeping her safe or just making it harder for her when she needs me.

That's the thing, isn't it? It's like, when you're just going to the grocery store or the library, do you really need your boss knowing the exact minute you left the drive-thru? But then if my kid gets sick or something happens, having that panic button is worth the privacy loss, I guess.
I mean, I guess that's the whole thing—sometimes I feel like I'm making a choice that hurts her more than it helps her.

Yeah, but honestly, I think the problem isn't turning it off completely, it's just being selective about who gets the live feed. Like, if the kid says "I'm lost," I want that to scream, but if they're just sitting in the library reading? Maybe that location shouldn't be pinging my phone every five minutes.
Yeah, but how do you decide which "selective" stuff is actually an emergency? Like, if she's just at the library two blocks away, is that urgent enough to wake me up, or do I need her to text first?
I mean, maybe she just needs to set a geofence so it only screams if she's actually miles away from home?

Yeah, but geofences are kinda hard to set up if you don't know where she's actually going most of the time, and if I have to wait for her to text me first, then by the time I get the message she's already two blocks away.
Yeah, but then you're just waiting around wondering if she's even gone to the library yet, and by the time you realize she's missing, she could be ten miles down the road.
I mean, maybe the app would just let you set those zones manually so you don't have to guess where she usually goes?
Yeah, exactly, just tell me where she's headed and I'll let her text me, but not every time she opens a book.
Yeah, that's the scary part—you don't even know if the zone is big enough to keep her safe but small enough to keep it private.
Yeah, but then you're just guessing where she might be, and if you get it wrong, you're not protecting her at all, you're just making her feel like she has to hide.
Yeah, but then she's just walking around thinking she has to sneak away from the library to get back to me, which feels like punishment for just going to read a book.
Yeah, but if she has to pretend she's working in the basement just to read her favorite section, that feels like we're winning the war on privacy but losing the war on trust.
Yeah, but if we're losing that trust to keep her safe, is there even a point in having her out at the library in the first place?

Look, maybe the problem is we're trying to control everything ourselves instead of just trusting her to text us when she actually needs help, and letting her be safe on her own for the rest of the time.
I mean, maybe that's the only way to do it, trust her enough not to set a zone at all and just let her come to me if she actually needs help.
Yeah, I guess that's where I want to be—let her come to me when she's actually scared, instead of trying to watch her every step.
Yeah, but if you don't watch her, who's gonna know she's missing until it's too late?

Yeah, but I think the real fix is just agreeing that we stop watching the minute-by-minute stuff and only look if she actually says she's in trouble, so we don't end up both terrified and distrustful.
